catalog_quote: Pamosu can be classified as a prototypical “stress language”, i.e. a language in which distinctive tone plays no part but which has word level stress. Every word of two syllables or more has contrastive stress on one syllable. Stress is placed in accordance with stress assignment rules which are predictable to speakers ... Given that stress is not phonemically significant, the following description of stress patterns in Pamosu is confined to a few general principles which are apparent from recorded texts. These principles represent generalisations only; every principle is contradicted by counter-examples, as discussed below. (a) Words ending in closed syllables generally take stress on the final syllable. ... (50) /kuɺɛnd/ [ku.ˈɺɛnd] ‘adze’ ... /mɔɸuβin/ [mɔ.ɸu.ˈβin] ‘they will not come’ (b) Two-syllable words ending in an open syllable generally take stress on the initial syllable. (51…

new_statements.quote: In Pamosu as well, stress is mostly predictable, and depends on the length of a word, its morphological makeup, and the structure of the final syllable (open or closed). Generally speaking, there is final stress on words with closed final syllables, and antepenultimate stress on words with open final syllables (Tupper 2012: 99-102). However, Tupper notes that there are numerous exceptions, for example itu 'flower' [i.ˈtu], which has an open final syllable but nonetheless has final stress.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds a Pamosu record with an empty rule and no existing statements, so this is the first placement statement held by the project: a weight-sensitive rule (closed final syllable -> final stress; open final syllable -> antepenultimate stress) with morphological conditioning and lexical exceptions. It is a secondary report of Tupper 2012: 99-102, which is the primary source to obtain.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is largely predictable from word length, morphology and the shape of the final syllable: a closed final syllable attracts final stress; with an open final syllable stress is antepenultimate. Numerous lexical exceptions exist (e.g. itu 'flower' with final stress despite an open final syllable). Pick reports this secondhand from Tupper 2012 (A Grammar of Pamosu, La Trobe PhD), pp. 99-102, and adds no data of his own.
new_statements.exceptions: 'numerous exceptions', with the example itu 'flower' [i.ˈtu] (open final syllable, yet final stress); footnote 11 (p. 32) contrasts Pamosu ('stress placement generally follows certain patterns, but has exceptions') with Usan, where Reesink 1987 calls stress phonemic.
new_statements.identity_note: Pick 2020 treats Pamosu as a Tibor language of the Northern Adelbert group and states that his Pamosu summary is 'based entirely on Tupper (2012)'; no dialect is specified. The 2002 SIL OPD is tagged for Pamosu [hih] (no dialect given on the landing page).

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding passage and every ancillary locator (2.3.1 pp. 99-101, 2.1 no length contrast, 4.1.2 p.195 stress shift) are verbatim in the Tupper 2012 text we hold; Deciding source: an 866-page 2012 PhD reference grammar with an explicit stress section, the only grammar of the language; the sole alternative is a 5-page 2002 SIL OPD draft (not fetchable now: sil.org and pnglanguages.sil.org return not reachable by automated download to scripted downloads; the Internet Archive has the record page but not the PDF). Coding 'weight-hedged' (final CVC attracts stress; otherwise initial in disyllables / antepenult in longer words; every principle hedged 'generally' with listed counter-examples) is a faithful rendering of Tupper's (a)-(c) plus his 'numerous exceptions' caveat, and Pick 2020: 31-32 (held) restates the same generalisation from the same pages.
